Gauteng Oncology Crisis

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A huge backlog at Gauteng Radiation Oncology Units means that public healthcare patients are often simply sent home to die

Unique Selling Point:
Gauteng's Public Oncology facilities have been strained for a number of years. Only about 20% of our Oncology specialists serve 85% of oncology patients in South Africa. In Gauteng, we only have 3 public radiation facilities -- Charlotte Maxeke, Baragwanath and Steve Biko -- but these three facilities have not been running optimally for years. Old equipment, untrained staff and a general lack of resources have plagued the departments. In April this year Charlotte Maxeke hospital was ravaged by a fire, and both the chemotherapy and radiation departments had to shut down. Patients were diverted to Steve Biko, which already only does Radiation treatment 2 days a week. Before the fire, the radiation waiting list was about 3,000 patients long for Gauteng. The fire and subsequent closure of the facilities meant that many patients' treatment were interrupted -- with oncology, the treatment regime is only effective if adhered to strictly, so it meant that many patients had to start over.

Summary:
On Tuesday 23 November 2021, a coalition of organisation -- including Section27, TAC and Cancer Alliance -- will march to Health MEC Dr Nomathemba Mokgethi's office, demanding action from the provincial Department of Health. Thousands of public cancer patients are suffering and not getting the treatment they deserve because of years-long mismanagement of the public health sector. As is, oncology patients in the public sector are usually only diagnosed at stage 3 and 4. They usually need urgent and reliable treatment and more often than not this is not available. A patient with Stage 4 cancer will not survive the 3-5 year waiting period to get their radiation treatment. Doctors in the public sector say they often just send patients home to die. At the same time there are over 50 private radiation facilities in Gauteng, may of then under-utilised, since they only cater for about 15% of cancer patients in the province. NGO's have called for PPP's but the department seems reluctant to accept.

Further information:
In Southern Africa there has been a marked increase in cancers linked to HIV, like cervical cancer and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. But as more people need specialised oncology treatment, it seems that facilities are deteriorating and the lack of specialised staff within the public sector is further putting strain on the situation.

Jodi Wishnia, public health consultant at Percept, says that their modelling work done between 2017 and 2019, shows that the number of oncological medical specialists in the sector was significantly lower than the need. “We found that in 2019, there were 146 radiation oncologists active in South Africa, 107 of these in the private sector and 39 in the public sector.” This meant that there was a ratio of 0.25 radiation oncologists for every 100 000 people living with cancer in the country, whereas Percept’s calculated target should be about five times more at around 1.28."

Charlotte Maxeke reopened on 28 June 2021, but sources say the facilities are still not running at 100% capacity, which means the waiting lists are growing by the day.

Script:


GAUTENG ONCOLOGY CRISIS


March visuals
V/O
Late in November last year a group of activists from various NPO’s took to the streets of Johannesburg to draw attention to the ongoing crisis in Oncology Radiation in Gauteng.
Linda Greeff
The issue is that there are nearly 3000 patients on the waiting list for radiation.


V/O
The March was organised by The Cancer Alliance. Chairperson, Linda Greeff says the situation in Gauteng is becoming a humanitarian emergency.
Linda Greeff
How long must we keep on asking for action to be taken before we don't have a even worse than Esidimeni crisis on our hands? In fact, I think we do have it, but it's just being denied.


LINK
When it comes to public healthcare in Gauteng there are only 2 radiation oncology units. One is at the Steve Biko Academic Hospital in Pretoria and the other is here at the Charlotte Maxeke Johannesburg Academic Hospital. The reality is it is not enough for the ever growing list of cancer patients.
V/O
Gauteng Health and Charlotte Maxeke Hospital officials gave us access to the Radiation Oncology Department. Dr Duvern Ramiah has been at the helm of this Unit since the end of February last year.
Dr Duvern Ramiah
00:04:37:27 - 00:05:10:05
So at the moment, the waiting list is quite long, some of our breast cancer patients with the waiting list can go up to 18 months and some of our prostate cancer patients can go up to up to five years for full treatment.
V/O
He says the backlog has been growing steadily since 2018...
Dr Duvern Ramiah
00:05:41:08 - 00:06:15:03
To give you an idea, we only have capacity to treat about five to six prostate cancer patients a month in this unit, and we get referred probably between 30 and 40 new patients for prostate cancer treatments a month.
V/O
Around 100,000 new cancer patients are diagnosed annually in South Africa, and the fact is many will end up here at Charlotte Maxeke for treatment...
Louise Turner
00:05:19:18 - 00:05:51:18
The biggest challenge we have currently is that the radiation oncology services in the county and particularly in Johannesburg, has collapsed.
V/O
Louise Turner runs the Breast Health Foundation, an NPO that focusses on awareness, education and support. She and her team work closely with the Breast Clinic at Helen Joseph Hospital in Johannesburg.
Louise Turner
0:01:41:10 - 00:02:12:02
It shouldn't be about where you live and what you earn to access treatment. I had my chemotherapy at the then Jhb Gen, Charlotte. I had my chemotherapy there 17 years ago. I'm here today.


V/O
But almost 2 decades on, Joburg’s flagship public hospital is buckling under the pressure of increased patient demand, budget cuts and bureaucracy...
Dr Duvern Ramiah
They are just four radiation oncologists in this unit to cope to to manage the treatment of about four thousand radiation patients a year. The doctors here at the moment are pushing patients through onto treatment, but they are doing much more and managing far more patients than should actually be safely managed by my radiation oncologist annually.
V/O
But even with doctors going beyond the call of duty, patients are falling through the cracks when it comes to radiation oncology...
Louise Turner
We've got over 300 patients from this unit from 2018 19 that are still waiting.
V/O
Denise Christie… A young mother from Springs in Gauteng is one of them...
Denise Christie
00:00:00:09 - 00:00:06:02
Claire: So let's go right back to the beginning, when were you first diagnosed with cancer?
26 of August 2020.


V/O
Denise has been battling breast cancer for 15 months...
Denise Christie
I had to undergo chemotherapy, six sessions, and then I had my lumpectomy in February and thereafter I should have gone for radiation and I should have been in remission by then.
LOUISE
After surgery patients have an estimated 3-month window to start radiation to stop the tumor from growing And the scary thing is, if you don't get to radiation in time, there's a very high likelihood of having a local recurrence that cancer growing back in that area. And once that happens, you start at the beginning and you go back to chemotherapy for six months, then another surgery, then you go onto the waiting list for radiation.
V/O
This is exactly what happened to Denise. Her cancer returned aggressively… What started as a small blister on her skin, which could have been treated with radiation, rapidly grew into a massive tumor that literally burst through the tissue of her breast… For the second time she had to undergo surgery. This time the entire breast was removed.
Denise Christie
Claire: Were you supposed to get radiation after your surgery?
Yes.


V/O
But for a second time she did not receive any radiation treatment…
A fire at Charlotte Maxeke Hospital in April 2021, meant that the Radiation Unit had to close down for 3 months.
Dr Duvern Ramiah
The fire sort of exacerbated issues that were already existing..
V/O
Fortunately the fire damage was limited mostly to the structure of the hospital and the Unit’s expensive state-of-the-art Linear Accelerator - or LINAC - machines survived the blaze.


Dr Duvern Ramiah
Claire: How many patients can get treatment on this machine in a day, for example?

A patient’s treatment takes about 15 minutes, so given the number of working hours in a day on average we treat about 35 to 40 patients…
V/O
While Dr Ramiah is obviously passionate about public healthcare and advancing oncology treatment here at Charlotte Maxeke, he and his team are faced with many challenges...
Dr Duvern Ramia
So there's only four external beam radiotherapy machines. When this unit initially was commissioned, it had seven. And so you can imagine that the number of patients has grown in the past 15-16 years, but the amount of equipment to treat the patients on it has gone down.
V/O
And then there are issues like loadshedding. Yes, power cuts affect the productivity of the Linac machines - they are simply not designed to be constantly switched on and off...
Dr Duvern Ramiah
00:20:14:21 - 00:20:47:22
All of them on a generator, but unfortunately it's not a seamless connection. So when the wind is load shedding, there is about a 20 30 second delay and that unfortunately does need the machine to be recalibrated when it comes online again.
V/O
The hospital has space for two additional compact LINAC systems, in bunkers where obsolete cobalt machines are waiting to be decommissioned… but it takes money and patience…
Dr Duvern Ramiah
We've gone through the process of putting through what's what equipment we need, and, you know, we're awaiting bidding and tendering and a process that's going to take years.


LINK
Traditionally Africa’s biggest health concerns have always been HIV, TB and Malaria but it is now said that Cancer is an emerging problem for the continent and cancer deaths are projected to exceed the global average by 30% in 20 years.
Portia Tsukudu
05:07 – Cancer is something we used to know as a white person’s thing. So when I got it it came as a big shock to me. And I told myself I am probably going to die. But by the grace of God i am still alive.
V/O
Portia Tshukudu was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2018. Her rapidly deteriorating health meant that she could not work and like so many others she used the little money she had to go look for medical treatment. She had chemo and a mastectomy … and by the end of 2019 she was due to get radiation, but she was simply told to wait…
Portia Tsukudu
Claire: so when you’re waiting all this time for radiation you don’t know why… they didn’t tell you…
04:46 – No, niks, I went to 348 (Oncology Radiation Department) for checkups. I asked them, but I never received a call from them.
V/O
But Portia is said to be one of the lucky ones, as she finally did get her radiation at the beginning of 2021… after a 16 month wait. But not everyone is that fortunate...
Portia Tsukudu
Claire: Do you know that some people, while they are waiting for radiation they get more sick?

09:04 – yes because there was a guy who died that day. He came for radiation treatment and he died right there on the chair.


Louise Turner
0:08:52:26 - 00:09:15:02
Claire: Explain that psychological impact of a patient knowing that they need radiation and they are not getting it and they waiting week after week, month after month. And it sounds like in some cases, year after year, they're still waiting.
These women are at their wits end. They phone us as their navigators and as their supporters, and they go, my son is five years old who's going to look after him. I'm going to die. And it's the fear that they live with every day because they know that last part of treatment they need is not coming their way.
V/O
In September Denise’s cancer returned for a third time...
Denise Christie
We went for a CT scan and we saw that it actually spread to my lymph nodes and I had some liquid on my lungs.


V/O
Realising she’s running out of time, the family is trying to raise enough money to afford private medical treatment.
Denise Christie
I just try to think of my husband and kids that still needs me. I need to fight this.
Dr Duvern Ramiah
Claire: I’ve spent not even an hour in your life and I’m overwhelmed, how do you not get overwhelmed?
Look it’s difficult and it’s difficult, like I said, for the doctors not becoming disheartened working here. You know, so it takes a special person to work in this unit...
V/O
Radiation Oncology is just the latest in a long list of failings within the Gauteng Health Department, which we have been persistently reporting on for many years. But despite the odds stacked against him, Dr Ramiah firmly believes this unit can be successfully turned around...






---- END ----


PROMO 1 11”
Years of equipment and staff shortages in the public health sector… means that the waiting list for oncology radiation in Johannesburg now runs into the thousands. Are we sending people home to die?




PROMO 2 21”
Cancer is synonymous with an expensive and exhausting treatment journey, but imagine having to do it twice, or even three times just because you couldn’t access the right treatment the first time? This is the reality for many of Gauteng’s public oncology patients as the waiting list for radiation has grown into the thousands and the number of oncologists has dwindled to a mere handful.




PROMO 3 21”
Charlotte Maxeke Johannesburg Academic Hospital has the only public oncology radiation unit in Southern Gauteng … and it’s struggling. The waiting list runs into the thousands and patients are suffering. But are the handful of caring professionals enough to turn things around?

UPSOUND RAMIAH: This unit has the potential of being the best oncology unit in in Africa. And it should be, you know, we just need more equipment,

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A huge backlog at Gauteng Radiation Oncology Units means that public healthcare patients are often simply sent home to die
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Gauteng's Public Oncology facilities have been strained for a number of years. Only about 20% of our Oncology specialists serve 85% of oncology patients in South Africa. In Gauteng, we only have 3 public radiation facilities -- Charlotte Maxeke, Baragwanath and Steve Biko -- but these three facilities have not been running optimally for years. Old equipment, untrained staff and a general lack of resources have plagued the departments. In April this year Charlotte Maxeke hospital was ravaged by a fire, and both the chemotherapy and radiation departments had to shut down. Patients were diverted to Steve Biko, which already only does Radiation treatment 2 days a week. Before the fire, the radiation waiting list was about 3,000 patients long for Gauteng. The fire and subsequent closure of the facilities meant that many patients' treatment were interrupted -- with oncology, the treatment regime is only effective if adhered to strictly, so it meant that many patients had to start over.
metadata.Summary: On Tuesday 23 November 2021, a coalition of organisation -- including Section27, TAC and Cancer Alliance -- will march to Health MEC Dr Nomathemba Mokgethi's office, demanding action from the provincial Department of Health. Thousands of public cancer patients are suffering and not getting the treatment they deserve because of years-long mismanagement of the public health sector. As is, oncology patients in the public sector are usually only diagnosed at stage 3 and 4. They usually need urgent and reliable treatment and more often than not this is not available. A patient with Stage 4 cancer will not survive the 3-5 year waiting period to get their radiation treatment. Doctors in the public sector say they often just send patients home to die. At the same time there are over 50 private radiation facilities in Gauteng, may of then under-utilised, since they only cater for about 15% of cancer patients in the province. NGO's have called for PPP's but the department seems reluctant to accept.
metadata.Further information: In Southern Africa there has been a marked increase in cancers linked to HIV, like cervical cancer and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. But as more people need specialised oncology treatment, it seems that facilities are deteriorating and the lack of specialised staff within the public sector is further putting strain on the situation. Jodi Wishnia, public health consultant at Percept, says that their modelling work done between 2017 and 2019, shows that the number of oncological medical specialists in the sector was significantly lower than the need. “We found that in 2019, there were 146 radiation oncologists active in South Africa, 107 of these in the private sector and 39 in the public sector.” This meant that there was a ratio of 0.25 radiation oncologists for every 100 000 people living with cancer in the country, whereas Percept’s calculated target should be about five times more at around 1.28." Charlotte Maxeke reopened on 28 June 2021, but sources say the facilities are still not running at 100% capacity, which means the waiting lists are growing by the day.
